title: The Mummy's Curse
objective: After this level you can explain where the legend of the mummy's curse came from.
summary: When Lord Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite in 1923, newspapers blamed a curse, a plot fiction had already written. A 2002 study found no evidence for it.

cards.headline: Tutankhamun’s tomb supposedly cursed its openers. Its excavator lived to 1939.
cards.body: Howard Carter, who led the excavation, died in London at 64. For a pharaoh’s revenge, that’s a remarkably slow start. So where did the curse come from?

cards.headline: One death, many headlines
cards.body: In April 1923, Lord Carnarvon, Carter’s patron, died in Cairo. The cause was an infection after a mosquito bite he got while visiting the newly opened burial chamber. His death set off sensational newspaper stories about a mummy’s curse. An infected bite is a sad story. A pharaoh’s revenge is a headline.
cards.callout: Real cause: an infected mosquito bite

cards.headline: The plot was already written
cards.body: The curse wasn’t new. Mummy curses had appeared in fiction long before: back in 1869, Louisa May Alcott published a thriller called “Lost in a Pyramid; or, The Mummy’s Curse.” When Carnarvon died, the story was waiting. The newspapers just had to fill in the names.

cards.headline: Putting the curse on trial
cards.body: In 2002, a study in the BMJ, a medical journal, tested the legend. It compared Westerners who were exposed to the “curse” at the tomb with those who weren’t. The exposed group died at an average age of 70, and the difference was not significant. Verdict: no evidence of a curse. Mosquito, one. Pharaoh, zero.

mascot.line: When a legend meets a spreadsheet, the spreadsheet usually wins.

cards.headline: The curse: debunked
learned: Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite
Newspapers turned his death into a curse story
Mummy curses already existed in fiction, like Alcott’s 1869 tale
A 2002 BMJ study found no evidence of a curse

questions.prompt: What actually killed Lord Carnarvon in 1923?

options.label: A falling stone in the tomb
options.rationale: He died in Cairo, of illness.

options.label: Poison painted on the tomb walls
An infection after a mosquito bite
A snake bite in the Valley of the Kings
options.rationale: It was an insect, not a snake.

questions.explanation: Carnarvon died of infection after a mosquito bite, not of any curse.

questions.prompt: A 2002 BMJ study tested the mummy’s curse. What did it find?

options.label: No evidence that exposure shortened lives
Mould in the tomb caused several deaths
options.rationale: The study found no link at all.

options.label: Only Carnarvon was affected
options.rationale: It compared many people and found no effect.

questions.explanation: People exposed to the “curse” died at an average age of 70, with no significant difference from the others.

questions.prompt: The curse legend grew around Tutankhamun’s tomb; from Level 64, what had happened to virtually every other tomb in the Valley of the Kings?

options.label: Buried under the Aswan reservoir
options.rationale: That threat faced Abu Simbel, much later.

options.label: Sealed with a curse, as the legend says

questions.explanation: Virtually every tomb in the valley was emptied in ancient times; Tutankhamun’s is the famous one that escaped.
